content.text: As a preventative measure, this issue could be resolved by verifying that the user-provided MediaType is valid here:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-kernel-modeshape/src/main/java/org/fcrepo/kernel/modeshape/FedoraBinaryImpl.java#L163
The verification could be an attempt to parse the provided MediaType with:
com.google.common.net.MediaType.parse()
...and throw a new exception (package: org.fcrepo.kernel.api.exception) that is mapped into a "400 Bad Request" status to the client.
Exception mappers, package: org.fcrepo.http.commons.exceptionhandlers
This update will also require an additional integration test method added to:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-http-api/src/test/java/org/fcrepo/integration/http/api/FedoraLdpIT.java
Would not using a regular expression be sufficient?
Something like mentioned here:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25201083/regex-to-match-and-validate-internet-media-type
That's simple and straight forward and doesn't require a library...
: Agreed, although fickle, a regex could certainly work. In this case, the suggested Google library is already a dependency in the fcrepo-kernel-modeshape package:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-kernel-modeshape/pom.xml#L78
In either case, if you are interested in helping create a PR, whichever approach you select would be appreciated.

I'm not entirely sure about the need for a special exception. It involves a lot of changed to the Kernel API. Especially because it seems to be unnecessary to provide an exception mapper.
: to clarify, are you ok with the approach being suggested by
: The HTTP layer should respond with BAD REQUEST on invalid, unparsable Media Types. I aggree with
s proposal to implement the check in the HTTP Layer.
Here is her comment on this:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1272#issuecomment-353173508

One could put this check up a level at the HTTP layer - in the code before setContent() is called. Then one could use the JAX-RS MediaType method valueOf, which seems to serve the same purpose as the guava parse() method. Also, JAX-RS exceptions are available then, so the new one might not be necessary.
However, I would recommend additional, independent checks at the Modeshape Kernel API, in case another transport layer (other than HTTP) is added some day.
: would you be interested and available to move this update forward?
Yes, I can move this forward this week - probably Friday.
- I think that's a good idea to have a check at the modeshape kernel level as well.
Maybe we can avoid an additional Kernel Exception by combining content errors into a more general Exception class. The current PR results in to many changes. Probably an "improvement" ticket...
I was talking with a colleague and he pointed out what's below, from
https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1341#page-56.

It seems like we should accept any mime type and treat those we don't know as 'application/octet-stream'.  I don't think we do much with binary mime types internally to start with, so this should be a non-issue. But it does mean, if we want to follow this, that we should not throw an exception on ingest and instead not have an error being thrown on retrieving the binary with an invalidly formatted mime type (as in, let the content type be whatever and make sure the user can retrieve / delete the item).   Thoughts?

5. Upon encountering any unrecognized Content-
 Type, an implementation must treat it as if it had
 a Content-Type of "application/octet-stream" with
 no parameter sub-arguments. How such data are
 handled is up to an implementation, but likely
 options for handling such unrecognized data
 include offering the user to write it into a file
 (decoded from its mail transport format) or
 offering the user to name a program to which the
 decoded data should be passed as input.
 Unrecognized predefined types, which in a MIME-
 conformant mailer might still include audio,
 image, or video, should also be treated in this
 way.
Hi - I want to ack that the above mentioned rfc has been obsoleted by
https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2045#page-12

A few questions for you – how is fcrepo being run in the hyku stack? Is it tomcat?   I'm wondering because I can't really reproduce this issue (I thought I had earlier, but I was misunderstanding what I was looking at).   Tomcat seems to check the mime type syntax and rejects it if it's bad (400 bad request with a note of a syntax error in the request) - so that it doesn't even get to fcrepo server.

It's possible that the mime type gets corrupted in fcrepo and set to the string above, but I can't really see a point in the code where that type of corruption could happen, unless it's outside fcrepo (as in, it's in the data that the webserver passes in.)
Essentially I'm looking for a way to reproduce this error - any thoughts?
Thanks!
More on this – to do a PUT with an incorrect mime type is hard to do as  tomcat checks the content-type syntax and won't allow it to pass.  But to
change
the field ebucore:hasMimeType after the binary has been inserted will work and successfully demonstrates the issue.
On a GET, there is a mime-type check on the field ebucore:hasMimeType which is what is throwing the exception.  I'll see if can relax that end of things.
It seems like we should accept any mime type and treat those we don't know as 'application/octet-stream'
The application should accept any mime type, as long as it has valid syntax.

Yes, I'm in agreement there. The issue I see is that one can set ebucore:hasMimeType triple at any point in time - then we later check that that value is a valid MediaType and that's where the exception is thrown.

So here's the scenario I think that is happening:  someone PUTS a file with a mime-type.  It's probably a valid one or the PUT won't get through Tomcat's syntax checking.   After that file is ingested, the client changes the ebucore:hasMimeType to something invalid.

- do you know the Hyku code well enough to know if something like this is happening?  That's the only way I've been able to enter an invalid mime type - by updating the rdf triples after I've ingested it.

It does imply, then, that one must either 1) validate the ebucore:hasMimeType triple if present in a sparql update or 2) relax the code that retrieves the binary content (since that's where the exception is thrown).
I'm not clear on whether or not ebucore:hasMimeType implies strict checking that it is a syntactically valid mime type versus just a string.   I found
this
:  `The main MIME types as defined by IANA: e.g. audio, video, text, application, or a container MIME type.`

What I'd most like to know regarding hyku/hyrax is if it adds the binary and then updates the RDF on the binary.    My logic: when one calls PUT or POST on fedora and includes the mime type, it should trigger the exception there, if the mime type is bad.  That's because this line:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-http-api/src/main/java/org/fcrepo/http/api/FedoraLdp.java#L370

invokes the MediaType.valueOf(String) constructor which checks syntax.  So if it was syntatically invalid going in, the exception would have happened there.  (MediaType.valueOf(String) is the method that's throwing the error when one tries to GET the binary later on.)
That leaves the idea that something is updating the ebucore:hasMimeType RDF triple in between.
may have some input on the details of Samvera; but it sounds like your suspicion that the mime-type is effectively corrupted on a subsequent PATCH request is likely the case.
If we can throw an exception on bad PATCHes, that would be helpful.
After that file is ingested, the client changes the ebucore:hasMimeType to something invalid.
- do you know the Hyku code well enough to know if something like this is happening?
I'm sorry
, I have no idea about Hyku. But I think your observation clearly indicates that it is possible to corrupt ebucore:hasMimeType.
Here is a PR that will solve the immediate problem.
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1280
A work around for this issue is to change the 'ebucore:hasMimeType' value to something syntactically valid. You should be able to retrieve the resource then.
Resolved by
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/commit/80ada4ae53804ff2885ab6e773c2f855f2fe3e76
This issue is not fully addressed yet.  There are two aspects to this ticket:
Degrade gracefully if an existing repository has bad mime type values (Bethany's PR, now merged addresses this)
Ensuring that bad values do not get in to the repository in the first place

We can debate if (2) is necessary - is it the responsibility of the repository to ensure that mime type values are syntactically correct?  If not, then this needs to be positively asserted and/or documented and this ticket can be closed.
If validation
is
necessary, then there are two areas of concern:
Validation of Content-Type headers in requests that create or modify an LDP-NR
Validation of direct mutations ebucore:hasMimeType triple (e.g. via a PATCH or PUT to the LDP-RS that describes an LDP-NR.)

Validation concern (2) is particularly problematic.  The modeshape implementation chooses to assign particular significance to the  ebucore:hasMimeType triple.  The value of this triple is used in crafting responses to GET or HEAD requests on the associated LDP-NR.  We speculate that Hyrax (or some associated service) was causing the problem via PATCH (
- can you confirm, please?).

While I cannot say for sure what was causing the invalid mimetype to be submitted to Fedora from Hyku, based on the investigation that Bethany has done, I would agree that a PATCH request is the most likely cause. This call likely occurred during a background job, after the initial ingest, where FITS is used for file characterization. Something likely went wrong during this processing step, but the call to update the mimetype in Fedora went forward.
Thanks,
.   I think, then, what we mainly need to decide is on whether or not we want to do this:
Validation of direct mutations ebucore:hasMimeType triple (e.g. via a PATCH or PUT to the LDP-RS that describes an LDP-NR.)
I think we're protected well enough against syntactically incorrect Content-Type headers all ready (with out any change to the code base).
Do we edit other string literals anywhere?  Would this be a new practice?  Those are the questions that pop into my mind.

We've also been seeing problems with the mime type being set to something invalid making a file inaccessible. One thing I noticed was that GET requests were returning the stack trace as the body of the 500, but the Hyrax side was issuing a HEAD request, which omits the body entirely. This made it a pretty silent error on the app side.

In our case, it was netCDF files being characterized as "application/netcdf, application/x-netcdf" by FITS/Droid. This resulted in a java.text parse error being thrown by Jersey, where it expected a {{;}} and got a  {{, }}– looking for options, not a secondary type.
I've opened an issue and pull request for this particular case on the hydra-works gem:
https://github.com/samvera/hydra-works/issues/334

In testing with the Hyku repository app on top of Fedora (using a build from the master branch, May 2017), occasional errors occur when files are deposited but fail to complete the process properly. When attempting to retrieve or delete the item from Fedora, a 500 response is returned. The errors in the log are:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Error parsing media type 'cannot open `/tmp/40e8273e-1ea8-48ec-916c-e78bc06ba1ea20170608-25523-m6g42x' (No such file or directory)'
followed by:
Caused by: java.text.ParseException: White space not allowed.
Requesting fcr:metadata on the item shows the following:
ebucore:hasMimeType      "cannot open `/tmp/40e8273e-1ea8-48ec-916c-e78bc06ba1ea20170608-25523-m6g42x' (No such file or directory)" ;

The mimetype set here is clearly invalid. While it seems likely that the primary issue is due to the Hyku app supplying an invalid mimetype, there should be better data validation in Fedora to ensure that a mimetype which cannot be parsed is not allowed into the repository.

Alternatively, if it is desirable to allow invalid data to be stored, then the API should fail gracefully when that data is requested and allow the item or the metadata itself to be removed or updated without error.
